Too polite, maybe. He said our proposal was interesting. It sounds like he did not like it.
I agree. When a British banker says interesting, you need to read between the lines.
And he said the timeline was a bit ambitious. That seems to be an understatement.
Exactly. He was implying that a closing in March is impossible.

Hello Aguinaldo, it's Emma Clarke from Thames Capital. Thank you for sending the new proposal. I've had a quick look, and it's certainly an interesting approach. The timeline is perhaps a little ambitious, and I'm not entirely sure that our committee will be comfortable with the guarantee as it is. But I'm sure we can find a way. Perhaps we could have a short call on Thursday to talk it through? Do let me know what works for you. Thanks very much.

When people learn English, they learn every word separately. But native speakers do not speak in separate words. They join them. Want to becomes wanna. Going to becomes gonna. Did you becomes didja. This is called connected speech, and it is the main reason why people with very good grammar still say that they cannot understand native speakers. The good news is that the patterns are limited. If you learn twenty of them, you will start to hear words that you thought were not there. My advice is simple. Do not listen for every word. Listen for the stressed words. They carry the meaning.

A language school in London asked five hundred international professionals about British business English, and the results were surprising. More than half of them said that they had misunderstood a British colleague at least once because of an understatement. The most confusing phrase was with the greatest respect, which usually means I think you are wrong. In second place was quite good, which can mean not very good. The director of the school says that the problem is not the words, but the tone. Her advice is simple: if you are not sure, ask. A polite question is always better than a wrong guess.
